drills.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2 and can't run on HTTP/1.1?
drills.a: gRPC needs trailing headers to carry the final grpc-status after the body (outcome unknown until the handler finishes), and needs true multiplexed independent streams for concurrent RPCs plus native bidirectional streaming -- both are HTTP/2-native (trailers frame, independent stream IDs) and neither is reliably available on HTTP/1.1.

drills.q: Walk through the protobuf wire format for a single int32 field, encoding field 1 = 150.
drills.a: Tag byte = (field_number<<3)|wire_type; field 1, wire type 0 (varint) = 0x08. Value 150 varint-encoded: 7 bits payload/byte, MSB=continuation flag, little-endian groups -- 150 needs 2 bytes: 0x96 0x01. Full encoding: 08 96 01, 3 bytes total.

drills.q: Give one safe .proto change and one that silently corrupts data.
drills.a: Safe: adding a new field with a new field number (old clients ignore it, new clients get a default if talking to an old server). Corrupting: reusing a field number for a different field after removal -- an old message deserialized with the new meaning applied to old bytes produces wrong data with no error thrown, since the parser never validates a number's historical meaning.

drills.q: Why does length-delimited (wire type 2) encoding matter for schema evolution?
drills.a: It lets a parser skip over an unrecognized field number by reading its length prefix and jumping past the bytes without understanding their meaning -- exactly what lets an old client safely ignore new fields a newer server added, which is the mechanism underlying forward compatibility.

drills.q: What's the difference between a gRPC deadline and a plain per-call timeout?
drills.a: A deadline is an absolute point in time set once by the originating client and auto-propagated as metadata through every downstream call derived from that request's context. A per-call timeout is independently set at each hop with no shared knowledge, so a chain of slow-but-under-timeout hops can collectively blow past what the original caller actually wanted.

drills.q: Explain cancellation propagation and name a concrete failure to watch for.
drills.a: Cancelling the parent context cancels every derived child call, so downstream services stop doing work nobody's waiting on. Failure to watch for: a downstream call made with a fresh/unrelated context instead of a derived one keeps running after the parent is gone -- wasting resources and, for a write, potentially completing a side effect the caller thinks never happened. Detect via tracing: a downstream span outliving the parent's cancellation timestamp is a propagation bug.

drills.q: Name the 4 gRPC RPC types and a real use case for each.
drills.a: Unary: fetch-a-record calls. Server-streaming: subscribing to live updates or consuming a large result incrementally (log tail, price feed). Client-streaming: uploading chunks with one final ack (chunked upload, batched telemetry). Bidirectional streaming: interactive, independently-paced exchange (chat-like protocols, live audio-to-text, multi-turn tool-call coordination).

drills.q: Why is UNAVAILABLE different from INTERNAL, and why does that distinction matter for retry policy?
drills.a: UNAVAILABLE signals the server/dependency was transiently unreachable -- safe to retry with backoff. INTERNAL signals an unexpected internal error/invariant violation -- retrying blindly rarely helps and may just repeat whatever triggered the bug. A retry policy treating every non-OK code the same either wastes resources retrying bugs or fails to retry things that safely could succeed.

drills.q: What does google.rpc.Status give you beyond a bare gRPC status code, and why not just use a detailed message string?
drills.a: Structured, typed error details (e.g. BadRequest listing which fields failed validation, RetryInfo suggesting a backoff) so a client can programmatically branch on rich error content. A message string is brittle across text/localization changes; typed details are a stable, versioned contract like the rest of the schema.

drills.q: When would you choose REST over gRPC for a new service, and would you unify on one API style for maintenance simplicity?
drills.a: When consumers are browsers or third-party developers needing to curl the endpoint, read human-readable JSON, and benefit from standard HTTP caching -- none of which gRPC gives without extra proxying (gRPC-Web). No, don't unify for maintenance convenience alone: maintaining two styles (gRPC internal, REST at the public edge) is a real ongoing cost that buys a materially better external developer experience -- collapsing to one style trades that away for engineering convenience, which is a product decision, not just an engineering one.

drills.q: A rolling deploy causes a burst of UNAVAILABLE errors, and separately one backend pod gets flooded with traffic afterward. Diagnose both.
drills.a: UNAVAILABLE burst: server likely closed connections during pod termination without draining in-flight RPCs or rejecting new ones gracefully, and/or the client's connection pool hadn't detected the backend was gone. Fix: graceful shutdown plus client-side retry with backoff on UNAVAILABLE. Flooded pod: gRPC's long-lived HTTP/2 connections mean a plain L4 load balancer only balances new connections, not individual requests -- clients reconnecting in a burst can pick unevenly. Fix: client-side or L7-aware (stream-level) load balancing.

drills.q: A field needs to change type from int32 to string. What do you do, and how do you version the API generally without breaking existing clients?
drills.a: You cannot change the existing field's type in place -- wire-incompatible, silently corrupts old data. Add a brand-new field with a new number and the new type, deprecate the old one, migrate readers/writers, then remove and reserve the old number. Generally prefer additive changes (new fields/numbers) within the same message over new service versions; reserve versioning at the package/service level (package myapi.v2) for genuinely breaking semantic changes, running both concurrently until clients migrate.
